summary: Extends IKEv2 so that more than one key exchange can contribute to the shared secret during security association setup, using the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange and a new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange for rekeying. It is aimed at hybrid and post-quantum key exchange.

plainLanguage.summary: IKEv2 sets up an encrypted tunnel by having both ends agree on a shared secret. This RFC lets them do that agreement more than once, using several different algorithms, and then combine the results so the tunnel survives even if one of the algorithms is later broken.

questions: how to do post-quantum key exchange in ikev2
what is ikev2 multiple key exchange
how does ikev2 support post-quantum key exchange
subtitle: How IKEv2 can run several key exchanges in a row so the session key survives a quantum computer.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 relies on Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, which are believed to be breakable by quantum computers, and post-quantum key exchanges are too new to trust alone and often too large for the first IKE message.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new transform types negotiate extra key exchanges, which run in IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges at security association setup and in the new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange for rekeying, with the session keys updated after each one.
tldr.outcome: The final keys depend on every exchange, so they stay secure if any one of them is secure. RFC 9370 updates RFC 7296.

facts.label: Payload size limit
facts.value: KE payloads over 64 KB are not addressed

today: RFC 9370 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2023. It updates RFC 7296 by renaming Transform Type 4 and the key exchange payload field. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it.

sections.title: Why the Existing Key Exchange Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2, as specified in RFC 7296, uses the Diffie-Hellman or the elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman algorithm, collectively called (EC)DH, to establish a shared secret between an initiator and a responder. The security of the (EC)DH algorithms relies on the difficulty of solving a discrete logarithm problem in multiplicative, and respectively elliptic curve, groups when the order of the group parameter is large enough.

While solving such a problem remains infeasible with current computing power, it is believed that general-purpose quantum computers will be able to solve it, which implies that the security of IKEv2 is compromised. There are, however, a number of cryptosystems that are conjectured to be resistant to quantum-computer attacks. This family of cryptosystems is known as post-quantum cryptography, sometimes also referred to as quantum-safe cryptography or quantum-resistant cryptography.

It is essential to be able to perform one or more post-quantum key exchanges in conjunction with an (EC)DH key exchange so that the resulting shared key is resistant to quantum-computer attacks. Since there is currently no post-quantum key exchange that is as well-studied as (EC)DH, performing multiple key exchanges with different post-quantum algorithms along with the well-established classical key-exchange algorithms addresses this concern, since the overall security is at least as strong as each individual primitive.
sections.plainLanguage: Quantum computers are expected to break Diffie-Hellman, the algorithm that lets two routers agree on a secret without sending it. Algorithms designed to resist quantum computers exist but are new and less tested. Doing both and combining them means the tunnel is only as weak as the strongest of the two.

sections.title: Combining Several Key Exchanges
sections.content:
This document describes a method to perform multiple successive key exchanges in IKEv2. The method allows integration of post-quantum cryptography in IKEv2 while maintaining backward compatibility, to derive a set of IKE keys that is resistant to quantum-computer attacks. It allows the negotiation of one or more post-quantum algorithms to exchange data, in addition to the existing (EC)DH key exchange data. The feature of using more than one post-quantum algorithm is important, because many of these algorithms are relatively new and there may be a need to hedge the security risk with multiple key exchange data from several distinct post-quantum algorithms.

IKE peers perform multiple successive key exchanges to establish an IKE security association. Each exchange produces a shared secret, and these secrets are combined in a way such that the final shared secret is computed from all of the component key exchange secrets; unless both peers support and agree to use the additional key exchanges, the final shared secret is equivalent to the one specified in RFC 7296; and if any part of the component key exchange method is a post-quantum algorithm, the final shared secret is post-quantum secure.

Some post-quantum key exchange payloads may have sizes larger than the standard maximum transmission unit size, so there could be issues with fragmentation at the IP layer. To allow those larger payload sizes, this mechanism relies on the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange specified in RFC 9242. The key exchange is initiated using a smaller, possibly classical, primitive such as (EC)DH, and then, before the IKE_AUTH exchange, one or more IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges are carried out, each of which contains an additional key exchange. Because the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange is encrypted, the IKE fragmentation protocol (RFC 7383) can be used.

The IKE SK values are updated after each exchange, so the final IKE security association keys depend on all the key exchanges, and the keys are secure if any of the key exchanges are secure. While the extension is primarily aimed at IKE security associations because of the fragmentation issue, it also applies to CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges for creating and rekeying Child SAs and for rekeying IKE SAs.

Readers should consider the approach as a long-term solution in upgrading IKEv2 to support post-quantum algorithms. A short-term solution is to use post-quantum pre-shared keys as specified in RFC 8784. The approach of performing multiple successive key exchanges is not limited to the threat of quantum computers; it can also be used when all the key exchanges are classical (EC)DH primitives and, for reasons such as policy requirements, it is essential to perform multiple key exchanges. The specification does not address key exchanges with KE payloads longer than 64 KB, because the current IKE payload format does not allow it.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra exchanges run inside encrypted IKE messages, which is what makes the large post-quantum payloads possible: the IKE fragmentation mechanism works there but not in the very first, unencrypted message. The keys are recomputed after each exchange so that the final key depends on all of them.

sections.title: Negotiating the Additional Exchanges
sections.content:
Multiple key exchanges are negotiated using the standard IKEv2 mechanism via the SA payload. Seven new transform types are defined: Additional Key Exchange 1 through 7, with ADDKE1 assigned the value 6 through ADDKE7 assigned the value 12. They are collectively called Additional Key Exchange transform types and have slightly different semantics from the existing IKEv2 transform types. They are interpreted as an indication of additional key exchange methods that peers agree to perform in a series of IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges following the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. The allowed transform IDs for these transform types are the same as the IDs for Transform Type 4, so they all share a single IANA registry for transform IDs.

The key exchange method negotiated via Transform Type 4 always takes place in the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. Additional key exchanges negotiated via the new transform types MUST take place in a series of IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges following the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, performed in the order of the values of their transform types, so that the key exchange negotiated using Additional Key Exchange i always precedes that of Additional Key Exchange i plus 1. Each additional key exchange method MUST be fully completed before the next one is started.

All of these transform types are optional, and the initiator is free to select any of them. If none are included in the proposal, the proposal indicates standard IKEv2 as defined in RFC 7296. If the initiator includes any of them, the responder MUST select one of the algorithms proposed using that type. A transform ID of NONE MAY be added to those transform types that contain key exchange methods which the initiator believes are optional according to its local policy. The responder's choice MUST NOT contain duplicated algorithms, except for the transform ID NONE. If the responder cannot select non-duplicated algorithms for each proposed key exchange, it MUST reject the message with an error notification of type NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. If the responder selects NONE for some of the transform types, the corresponding additional key exchanges MUST NOT take place. The initiator MAY propose transform types that are not consecutive, and the responder MUST treat all the omitted ones as if they had been proposed with transform ID NONE.

If the initiator includes any of the new transform types in the SA payload of the IKE_SA_INIT request, it MUST also negotiate the use of the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange by including an INTERMEDIATE_EXCHANGE_SUPPORTED notification in the same message. A responder that agrees MUST return that notification in its response. If the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange is not negotiated, the peers MUST treat any of the new transform types as unknown transform types and skip the proposals they appear in.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra exchanges are offered in the same proposal list the protocol already uses, so no new negotiation machinery is needed. Each of the seven slots is optional, and the responder may answer NONE in a slot to say that exchange is not wanted. The order of the slots fixes the order the exchanges run in.

sections.title: Running the Additional Exchanges
sections.content:
For each additional key exchange agreed to in the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, the initiator and the responder perform an IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange. The initiator sends key exchange data in its KE payload, protected with the current encryption and authentication keys, and the responder replies with its own key exchange payload, protected the same way. The former Diffie-Hellman Group Num field, now called the Key Exchange Method field, in those payloads MUST match the n-th negotiated additional key exchange.

Once each exchange is done, both sides compute updated keying material. The new seed is SKEYSEED(n) = prf(SK_d(n-1), SK(n) | Ni | Nr), where SK(n) is the resulting shared secret from this exchange, Ni and Nr are the nonces from the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, and SK_d(n-1) is the last generated SK_d, derived from IKE_SA_INIT for the first use of IKE_INTERMEDIATE and otherwise from the previous IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange. The other keying materials are generated from that seed as {SK_d(n) | SK_ai(n) | SK_ar(n) | SK_ei(n) | SK_er(n) | SK_pi(n) | SK_pr(n)} = prf+(SKEYSEED(n), Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr). Both the initiator and the responder use these updated key values in the next exchange, whether that is another IKE_INTERMEDIATE or the IKE_AUTH exchange.

After all the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges have completed, the initiator and the responder perform the IKE_AUTH exchange, which is the standard IKE exchange with the AUTH payload calculation modification described in RFC 9242.
sections.plainLanguage: After each key exchange, both sides mix the new shared secret into the seed for all the session keys and derive a fresh set of keys. So the keys change at every step, and by the last step they depend on every exchange that came before.

sections.title: Rekeying with IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE
sections.content:
The CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange is used in IKEv2 to create additional Child SAs, to rekey them, and to rekey the IKE SA itself. When creating or rekeying Child SAs, the peers may optionally perform a key exchange to add fresh entropy to the session keys; in the case of an IKE SA rekey the key exchange is mandatory. Using multiple key exchanges with a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange is negotiated in a similar fashion to the initial IKE exchange. If the initiator includes any of the new transform types in the SA payload and the responder agrees, the additional key exchanges are performed in a series of new IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchanges that follow the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. The IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange is introduced especially for transferring data of additional key exchanges following the one performed in the CREATE_CHILD_SA, and its Exchange Type value is 44.

After an IKE SA is created the window size may be greater than one, so several concurrent exchanges may be in progress. It is therefore essential to link the IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchanges together with the corresponding CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. A new status type notification called ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE is introduced for this purpose, with Notify Message Type value 16441 and Protocol ID and SPI Size both set to 0. The data is a blob meaningful only to the responder, so that the responder can link successive exchanges; for the initiator the content is an opaque blob. The responder MUST include this notification in a CREATE_CHILD_SA or IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE response when the next IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange is expected, and the initiator MUST send it back intact in the request of the next IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange.

Due to unexpected events such as a reboot, the initiator may lose its state and never start the remaining exchanges. The responder MUST handle this gracefully and delete the associated state if it does not receive the next expected request after some reasonable period; in general, 5 to 20 seconds of waiting time should be appropriate in most cases. If the responder receives an IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE message for which it has no key exchange state, it MUST send back a new error type notification called STATE_NOT_FOUND, whose Notify Message Type value is 47, with Protocol ID and SPI Size both set to 0 and empty data. This notification is not fatal to the IKE SA. If the initiator receives it in response to an IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE exchange performing an additional key exchange, it MUST cancel that exchange and treat the whole series started from the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange as having failed. It MAY start a new CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange to retry, but if it keeps receiving the notification after several retries it MUST treat the situation as fatal and delete the IKE SA by sending a DELETE payload.
sections.plainLanguage: When a tunnel is rekeyed, the extra exchanges run in a new message type. The responder needs a way to know which follow-up message belongs to which rekey request, so each reply carries an opaque token that the initiator echoes back in the next request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is intended to mitigate two possible threats in IKEv2: the compromise of the (EC)DH key exchange using Shor's algorithm while remaining backward compatible, and the potential compromise of existing or future post-quantum key exchange algorithms. To address the first threat, the extension allows the establishment of a shared secret by using multiple key exchanges, typically one classical (EC)DH and the other one post-quantum algorithm. To address the latter threat, multiple key exchanges using a post-quantum algorithm can be performed to form the shared key.

Unlike the key exchange method in Transform Type 4, the encryption algorithm in Transform Type 1, the pseudorandom function in Transform Type 2 and the integrity algorithm in Transform Type 3 are not susceptible to Shor's algorithm. They are, however, susceptible to Grover's attack, which allows a quantum computer to perform a brute force key search using quadratically fewer steps than the classical counterpart. Simply increasing the key length can mitigate this attack. It was previously believed that one needed to double the key length of these algorithms, but there are a number of factors that suggest it is quite unlikely to achieve the quadratic speedup using Grover's algorithm. According to NIST, current applications can continue using an AES algorithm with the minimum key length of 128 bits, although if the data needs to remain secure for many years to come one may want to consider a longer key size for the algorithms in Transform Types 1 to 3.

The SKEYSEED is calculated from the shared secret using an algorithm defined in Transform Type 2. While a quantum attacker may learn the value of a classically computed secret, other values generated by means of a post-quantum algorithm ensure that the final SKEYSEED is not compromised, assuming that the algorithm in Transform Type 2 is quantum resistant. The ordering of the additional key exchanges should not matter in general, since only the final shared secret is of interest, but because the strength of the running shared secret increases with every additional key exchange, an implementer may want to perform the most secure method first.

The main focus of the document is to prevent a passive attacker from performing a harvest-and-decrypt attack, where an attacker records messages exchanged today and decrypts them once they have access to cryptographically relevant quantum computers. Other attacks involving an active attacker using a quantum computer are not completely solved, for two reasons. The authentication step remains classical, so the authenticity of the security associations is protected by pre-shared keys or digital signature algorithms; while the pre-shared key option is post-quantum secure if the key is long enough, the other algorithms are not. Secondly, the purpose of post-quantum algorithms is to provide resistance to attacks mounted in the future, and the current threat is that encrypted sessions are archived and decrypted later; the authenticity of a connection only matters at the time of the connection, so there is less urgency for post-quantum authenticity than for post-quantum confidentiality.

Performing multiple key exchanges while establishing an IKE SA increases the responder's susceptibility to denial-of-service attacks, because more resources are needed before the initiator is authenticated. This is especially true for post-quantum key exchange methods, which are often more memory and CPU intensive than the classical ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel keys survive a quantum attack, but the proof of who is at the other end does not: that still uses a digital signature, and digital signatures are not yet post-quantum. The document also warns that the responder does more work before it knows who is calling, which is a denial-of-service risk.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document adds a new exchange type to the IKEv2 Exchange Types registry, the value 44 for IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE. It renames Transform Type 4 in the Transform Type Values registry from Diffie-Hellman Group to Key Exchange Method, and renames the IANA registry originally titled Transform Type 4 - Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs to Transform Type 4 - Key Exchange Method Transform IDs.

It adds seven transform types to the Transform Type Values registry: Additional Key Exchange 1 through 7, with values 6 to 12, each optional in IKE, AH and ESP. It defines a new notify message type in the IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Status Types registry, the value 16441 for ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE, and a new notify message type in the IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Error Types registry, the value 47 for STATE_NOT_FOUND.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers the seven new proposal slots, the new message type used for the follow-up exchanges, and the two notifications that link them together and report a lost exchange.

viz.caption: What the extension does and does not fix

items.title: Key agreement
items.text: Survives a quantum attack on Diffie-Hellman, because the final key depends on every exchange.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: Still classical, so a digital signature or pre-shared key protects the peer identity.

items.title: Encryption keys
items.text: Grover's attack still applies, so a longer key size may be wanted for long-lived data.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: The responder does more work before the initiator is authenticated.

viz.caption: The code points this document registers

items.label: IKE_FOLLOWUP_KE
items.desc: The new IKEv2 exchange type used for extra key exchanges.

items.label: ADDKE1 to ADDKE7
items.desc: The seven new transform types, one per additional key exchange.

items.label: ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE
items.desc: Status notification that links a follow-up exchange to its rekey request.

items.label: STATE_NOT_FOUND
items.desc: Error notification sent when a follow-up exchange arrives with no state.
